title: How do you solve a profitability case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete profitability case guide: the structure, a worked bakery case with real numbers, the mistakes that cost candidates, and practice prompts.
hook: You solve a profitability case by splitting profit into revenue and costs, finding the line that moved, explaining why it moved, and ending with a recommendation that says how much profit it wins back. The skill is in sizing the gap early and drilling into the right branch. This guide walks through the method and a full bakery case with every number shown.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet a profitability case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • The five steps from prompt to recommendation
  • A fully worked example: the bakery chain
  • A second pattern: revenue up, profit down
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet a profitability case

Profitability is the most common case type. It comes as "profits have fallen", "margins are shrinking", "we are growing but making less money" or "how can the client be more profitable?" A revenue decline case uses the same tree with more time on the revenue branch. The industry changes the drivers, not the logic.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Profit is revenue minus costs. Every useful profitability structure is a more detailed version of that line:

  • Revenue = units sold × price per unit
    • Units: number of customers × purchases per customer
    • Price: list price, discounts, and the mix of products sold
  • Costs
    • Fixed costs: rent, salaried staff, overheads
    • Variable costs: materials, delivery, commissions

Add two cuts to every branch. Segment each line by product, customer, channel and region, because a shift in mix often hides inside an average. And compare with competitors: if the whole industry is down, the cause is in the market; if only your client is, it is in the company.

The first question to ask, out loud, is:

Has revenue fallen, have costs risen, or both? And is the whole industry seeing this, or just our client?

The answers tell you which half of the tree to open first. For the tree itself in more depth, see how to use the profitability framework.

The five steps from prompt to recommendation

  1. Clarify the goal. Confirm which profit, the period and any target. "Back to last year" and "a 15% margin in three years" are different cases.
  2. Lay out the structure. Revenue and cost branches plus the segment and competitor cuts, only as deep as you will use. Our guide to structuring shows how to present it in under a minute.
  3. Size the gap. Ask for revenue and costs at both dates and work out how much of the change sits on each side. One subtraction saves ten minutes of wandering.
  4. Drill into the branch that moved. Find the item that explains most of the gap, then ask why it changed. The answer is usually customer or competitor behaviour, not an accounting line.
  5. Recommend, with the size of the prize. The cause, two or three actions, how much profit they recover, the main risk and the next step.

A fully worked example: the bakery chain

The prompt: a regional bakery chain's revenue has been flat at $20M for two years, but operating profit fell from $2.0M to $1.2M. Why, and what should it do? The figures below are illustrative.

Step 1: split the change

Profit fell by $0.8M. Revenue is flat, so the whole fall sits in costs: costs rose from $18.0M ($20M minus $2.0M) to $18.8M ($20M minus $1.2M). Ask for the cost lines:

Cost lineTwo years agoNowChange
Ingredients$6.0M$6.2M+$0.2M
Staff$7.0M$7.1M+$0.1M
Rent$2.0M$2.0M0
Delivery app commissions$0.5M$1.0M+$0.5M
Other$2.5M$2.5M0
Total$18.0M$18.8M+$0.8M

Step 2: find the driver

Commissions explain $0.5M of the $0.8M, or about 63%. The apps charge 25% of the order value, so commission doubling from $0.5M to $1.0M means delivery sales doubled from $2M to $4M. Total revenue did not grow, so in-store sales must have fallen by the same $2M, from $18M to $16M. Customers have moved from the counter to the app.

Step 3: the so-what

Delivery is not bringing new customers. It is the same customers, buying the same amount, with the bakery now paying 25 cents in commission on every dollar that moved. The other $0.3M (ingredients and staff) looks like normal inflation: flag it and move on.

Step 4: size the fixes

Two actions, each with its own maths:

  • Move some app customers to click-and-collect. If $1M of the $4M delivery sales switches to click-and-collect with a 5% discount, the bakery saves $1M × 25% = $0.25M of commission and gives up $1M × 5% = $0.05M of revenue. Net gain: $0.20M.
  • Raise delivery menu prices by 10%. On the remaining $3M of delivery sales, and assuming volume holds, revenue rises by $0.30M. The apps take 25% of that, so the bakery keeps $0.30M × 75% = $0.225M.

Together that is about $0.43M, just over half the $0.8M fall. The volume assumption is the risk, so say so.

Step 5: the recommendation

Profit fell by $0.8M mainly because $2M of sales moved from our shops to delivery apps, which take 25% commission without bringing extra revenue. I'd move app customers to click-and-collect with a small discount and raise delivery prices by about 10%. Together these recover roughly $0.4M a year. The main risk is losing delivery customers to rivals, so I'd test the price rise in a few shops first, and then check whether our ingredient costs are rising faster than competitors'.

A second pattern: revenue up, profit down

Suppose a software company grew revenue from $10M to $12M while operating profit fell from $2M to $1M. Costs rose from $8M to $11M: $3M of extra cost for $2M of extra sales. Split revenue into customers × revenue per customer: customers grew from 2,000 to 3,000, but revenue per customer fell from $5,000 to $4,000, a 20% drop. The company is buying growth, probably with discounts or smaller customers who may also cost more to serve.

Check the maths. If each of the extra 1,000 customers contributes $1,000 a year after variable costs, they add $1M; if sales, onboarding and support spending grew by $2M to win them, profit falls by $1M, which matches. That can still be a sound investment if the customers stay, so ask about churn and how long acquisition spending takes to pay back. The fix (tighter discounting, a standard onboarding package, fewer support tickets) depends on which segment destroys profit. Cutting staff across the board would be the weak answer.

Strong and weak answers

A weak candidate jumps to ideas:

The bakery could cut staff, renegotiate rent, launch new products and do more marketing.

None of it is tied to the cause, and rent did not even move. A strong candidate locates the problem first:

Revenue is flat, so the whole $0.8M sits in costs. Could I see the cost lines over the two years?
Commissions explain over 60% of the fall, so I'd like to understand the delivery channel next.

The difference is the habit of quantifying before brainstorming, and of saying what each number means.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Brainstorming before checking which side moved. Split the profit change into revenue and costs first.
  2. Treating revenue as one number. The bakery's problem was invisible until delivery and in-store were separated.
  3. Finding the driver but not the reason. "Commissions went up" is a fact. "The same customers now cost us 25% more to serve" is the insight.
  4. Forgetting the market. Check whether competitors show the same trend before you blame the client.
  5. Ending with a list. Give one cause, two or three actions, the profit they recover and the main risk.

Practise with these prompts

Take two minutes per prompt: a structure and where you would start.

A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show the answer
  • Market: total applications across all lenders, driven by interest rates, house prices and transactions. Is everyone down 20%, or just us?
  • Our offer: rates and fees against rivals, loan-to-value limits, product range.
  • Channels and process: are brokers placing fewer loans with us? Time to decision, approval rates and drop-off (brokers avoid slow or strict lenders).

Where to start: the market. If every bank is down 20%, the client's share is unchanged.

The trap: jumping to marketing ideas before checking whether the whole market fell.

A pharma company's new drug is selling 40% below forecast.

Show the answer
  • Doctors: awareness of and trust in the trial data; which doctors prescribe it (specialists or family doctors).
  • Patients: how many are diagnosed and eligible, and was the forecast realistic? Price, side effects, stopping early.
  • Payers: reimbursement approval, and restrictions such as "only after other drugs fail".
  • Competition: rival drugs, their pricing and contracts.

Where to start: payers. If insurers restrict the drug, doctors and patients can do little about it.

The trap: assuming it is a marketing problem when access and reimbursement usually decide.

Quick maths: revenue is flat at $50M, costs rose from $45M to $47M, and $1.5M of the rise is fuel. What share of the profit fall does fuel explain?

Show the answer

Profit fell from $5M to $3M, so fuel explains $1.5M ÷ $2M = 75% of the fall. Next, ask whether it came from price per litre or from distance travelled: the fixes differ.

Where to practise next

  • Run a full case: Coastal Brew (a growing coffee chain making less money) and Kettle & Crumb (a bakery that added products and lost profit).
  • Drill the opening: the first question and the trap in one page.
  • Practise structures at speed: 17 profitability and revenue decline prompts.
